knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

## Load R packages
```{r}
# Load required packages for DIABLO analysis
# mixOmics: provides multiblock supervised integration methods (DIABLO/block.splsda)
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/methods/diablo/
# Tutorial: http://mixomics.org/case-studies/diablo-tcga-case-study/
library(mixOmics)

# tidyverse: data manipulation and visualization tools
library(tidyverse)

# igraph: network analysis and export to Cytoscape
library(igraph)

# Set seed for reproducibility - critical for cross-validation and feature selection
set.seed(123)
```

## Import all omics
```{r}
# Import multi-omics datasets for DIABLO integration
# DIABLO (Data Integration Analysis for Biomarker discovery using Latent cOmponents)
# requires matched samples across all omics layers

# Transcriptomics: RNA expression data
Strep_trans_data <- read.csv("/Users/wmujchariyak/Desktop/Strep_transcriptome_data.csv", header = TRUE) %>% 
  column_to_rownames(var = "X")

# Proteomics: Protein abundance data
Strep_prot_data <- read.csv("/Users/wmujchariyak/Desktop/Strep_proteome_data.csv", header = TRUE) %>% 
  column_to_rownames(var = "X")

# Metabolomics: Metabolite concentration data (GC-MS)
Strep_met_GC_data <- read.csv("/Users/wmujchariyak/Desktop/Strep_metabolome_GC_data.csv", header = TRUE) %>% 
  column_to_rownames(var = "X")
```

## Data for MixOmics (DIABLO)
```{r}
# Prepare data in the format required for DIABLO analysis
# All datasets must have:
# 1. Same samples (rows) in the same order
# 2. Named list format for multi-block integration

data <- list(Transcript = Strep_trans_data, 
             Protein = Strep_prot_data, 
             Metabolite_GC = Strep_met_GC_data)

# Verify dimensions: all should have 60 rows (samples) but different columns (features)
lapply(data, dim)

# Define outcome variable (Y)
# This is the categorical variable we want to predict/discriminate
# RPMI = control medium, SERUM = experimental condition with serum
Y <- factor(rep(c("RPMI", "SERUM"), 30))

# Check class distribution (should be balanced: 30 RPMI, 30 SERUM)
summary(Y)
```

## Initial DIABLO model 
```{r}
# Create the design matrix - specifies how omics blocks should be connected
# The design matrix controls the level of correlation sought between datasets
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/methods/diablo/#design-matrix

# Initialize design matrix with 0.1 for all pairwise connections
# Values range from 0 (no connection) to 1 (maximum correlation)
# 0.1 is a moderate value that encourages some correlation between blocks
# while still allowing each block to maintain its individuality
design = matrix(0.1, 
                ncol = length(data), 
                nrow = length(data), 
                dimnames = list(names(data), names(data)))

# Set diagonal to 0 (blocks don't correlate with themselves)
diag(design) = 0

# View the design matrix
# This symmetric matrix shows connection strength between each pair of omics layers
design

# Key points about design matrix:
# - Higher values (closer to 1): seek stronger correlation between blocks
# - Lower values (closer to 0): allow blocks to be more independent
# - Common values: 0.1 (weak), 0.5 (moderate), 0.9 (strong)
```

## Tuning parameters
** [LOO-CV issue](https://mixomics-users.discourse.group/t/loo-cv-outputs-na-in-choice-ncomp/145/3) - you can look at the perf plot and decide on the number of components (Here, ncomp = 1).  
```{r}
# STEP 1: Tune the number of components (latent variables)
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/methods/diablo/#tune-number-components

# Create initial DIABLO model with arbitrarily high number of components
# block.splsda = multiblock sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis
# This is the core function for DIABLO analysis
# ncomp = 5: start with 5 components to evaluate optimal number
basic.diablo.model = block.splsda(X = data, Y = Y, ncomp = 5, design = design)

# Evaluate model performance using cross-validation
# perf() assesses classification performance for different numbers of components
# validation = 'loo': leave-one-out cross-validation (recommended for small datasets)
# Alternative: 'Mfold' for larger datasets
perf.diablo = perf(basic.diablo.model, validation = 'loo', nrepeat = 1) 

# Visualize performance metrics vs number of components
# Look for the point where error rate plateaus or increases
plot(perf.diablo)

# Extract optimal number of components based on lowest error rate
# "Overall.BER" = overall Balanced Error Rate (accounts for class imbalance)
# "centroids.dist" = distance metric used for classification
ncomp = perf.diablo$choice.ncomp$WeightedVote["Overall.BER", "centroids.dist"] 

# Display optimal ncomp for all distance metrics
# This helps verify consistency across different classification approaches
perf.diablo$choice.ncomp$WeightedVote 
```

```{r}
# Preliminary visualization of basic DIABLO model
# These plots help assess initial model quality before tuning

# Sample plot: shows how samples separate in multiblock latent space
plotIndiv(basic.diablo.model, ind.names=FALSE, legend=TRUE)

# Loadings plot: shows which features contribute most to each component
plotLoadings(basic.diablo.model)
```


## Tuning the number of features 
** This may take some time to run (~ 5 min)
```{r}
# STEP 2: Tune the number of features to retain per component
# This performs feature selection to identify the most discriminative variables
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/methods/diablo/#tune-keepx

# Define grid of feature numbers to test for each omics block
# These ranges represent the number of variables to select per component
test.keepX = list (Transcript = seq(20,100,20),      # Test 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 transcripts
                   Protein = seq(20,100,20),         # Test 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 proteins
                   Metabolite_GC = seq(10,100,10))   # Test 10, 20, 30, ..., 100 metabolites

# Note: Metabolites have smaller range because datasets typically have fewer metabolites
# seq(10,100,10) means: start at 10, increment by 10, stop at 100

# Run feature selection tuning - THIS IS COMPUTATIONALLY INTENSIVE
# tune.block.splsda tests all combinations in test.keepX to find optimal feature counts
# validation = 'Mfold': M-fold cross-validation (splits data into folds)
# folds = 5: use 5-fold CV (80% training, 20% testing in each iteration)
# nrepeat = 10: repeat CV 10 times with different random splits for robustness
# dist = "centroids.dist": classification based on distance to class centroids
tune.SA = tune.block.splsda(X = data, Y = Y, ncomp = 1, 
                              test.keepX = test.keepX, design = design,
                              validation = 'Mfold', folds = 5, nrepeat = 10,
                              dist = "centroids.dist")

# Extract optimal number of features for each block
# These values minimize classification error while maximizing model interpretability
list.keepX = tune.SA$choice.keepX 

# Display optimal feature counts
# Example output: Transcript: 40, Protein: 60, Metabolite_GC: 30
list.keepX
```


## Final DIABLO model
```{r}
# STEP 3: Build final DIABLO model with optimized parameters
# Use the optimal number of features identified from tuning
# (or choose manually based on biological relevance and interpretability)

# Specify number of features to retain from each omics block
# These are signature molecules that best discriminate between conditions
list.keepX <-  list (Transcript =  20,        # Select top 20 discriminative transcripts
                    Protein =  20,            # Select top 20 discriminative proteins
                    Metabolite_GC = 10)       # Select top 10 discriminative metabolites

# Build final DIABLO model with optimized parameters
# This model integrates all omics layers while maximizing:
# 1. Discrimination between RPMI and SERUM conditions
# 2. Correlation between selected features across omics layers
# 3. Feature sparsity (selecting only most relevant variables)
final.diablo.model = block.splsda(X = data, Y = Y, ncomp = 1, 
                                  keepX = list.keepX, design = design)

# Display design matrix used in final model
# Confirms the correlation structure between omics blocks
final.diablo.model$design
```

## AUC for final model
```{r}
# Calculate Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) to assess model performance
# AUC ranges from 0.5 (random) to 1.0 (perfect classification)
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/methods/diablo/#model-performance

# AUC for transcriptomics block, component 1
# roc.block specifies which omics layer to evaluate
# roc.comp specifies which component to evaluate
# print = FALSE suppresses detailed output
auc.diablo.trans.com <- auroc(final.diablo.model, 
                               roc.block = "Transcript", 
                               roc.comp = 1,
                               print = FALSE)

# AUC for proteomics block, component 1
auc.diablo.prot.com <- auroc(final.diablo.model, 
                              roc.block = "Protein", 
                              roc.comp = 1,
                              print = FALSE)

# AUC for metabolomics block, component 1
auc.diablo.met.GC.com <- auroc(final.diablo.model, 
                                roc.block = "Metabolite_GC", 
                                roc.comp = 1,
                                print = FALSE)

# Interpretation:
# AUC > 0.9: Excellent discrimination
# AUC 0.8-0.9: Good discrimination
# AUC 0.7-0.8: Fair discrimination
# AUC < 0.7: Poor discrimination
```

## Extract data from final DIABLO model 
```{r}
# Extract the selected discriminative variables from each omics block
# These are the "signature" molecules that best distinguish between conditions
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/methods/diablo/#variable-selection

# Extract selected transcripts from component 1
# Returns variable names and their contribution values
trans_var <- selectVar(final.diablo.model, block = 'Transcript', comp = 1)

# Extract selected proteins from component 1
prot_var <- selectVar(final.diablo.model, block = 'Protein', comp = 1)

# Extract selected metabolites from component 1
met_GC_var <- selectVar(final.diablo.model, block = 'Metabolite_GC', comp = 1)

# Extract correlation matrix between selected variables
# This matrix is used to generate the circos plot
# cutoff = 0.7: only show correlations with |r| > 0.7 (strong correlations)
corMat <- circosPlot(final.diablo.model, cutoff = 0.7)

# Convert correlation matrix to data frame for further analysis
# Useful for identifying highly correlated multi-omics modules
corMat2 <- as.data.frame(corMat)
```

## Data visualization
```{r}
# Visualize sample clustering in the integrated multi-omics space
# plotDiablo creates an arrow plot showing sample projections from each omics block
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/graphics/sample-plots/plotdiablo/

# Sample plots (arrow plot)
# Each panel shows samples from one omics block
# Arrows connect the same sample across different omics representations
# Samples that cluster together share similar molecular profiles
plotDiablo(final.diablo.model, ncomp = 1)

# Interpretation:
# - Consistent arrow directions: good agreement between omics layers
# - Sample separation: clear distinction between RPMI and SERUM conditions
# - Arrow length: magnitude of projection (longer = stronger signal)
```

```{r fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
# Visualize feature contributions (loadings) for each omics block
# Shows which variables contribute most to discrimination between conditions
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/graphics/variable-plots/plotloadings/

# Plot loadings for all blocks on component 1
# contrib = 'max': color bars by maximum contribution
# method = 'median': order features by median absolute loading value
# size.name = 0.65: adjust text size for feature names
plotLoadings(final.diablo.model, comp = 1, contrib = 'max', method = 'median', size.name = 0.65)

# Interpretation:
# - Bar length: strength of variable's contribution
# - Bar color: which class the variable is most associated with
# - These are the key discriminative features (biomarker candidates)
```


```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=10}
# Create circos plot to visualize correlations between selected variables
# This plot shows the multi-omics correlation network
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/graphics/variable-plots/circosplot/

# Circos plot parameters:
# cutoff = 0.9: only display correlations with |r| > 0.9 (very strong correlations)
# comp = 1: use correlations from component 1
# line = TRUE: draw lines representing correlations between variables
# color.blocks: assign colors to each omics block for visual distinction
#   - darkorchid: Transcripts
#   - brown1: Proteins  
#   - lightgreen: Metabolites
# color.cor: color scheme for correlation lines
#   - chocolate3: positive correlations
#   - grey20: negative correlations
# size parameters: control text and element sizes for readability
circosPlot(final.diablo.model, cutoff = 0.9, comp = 1, line = TRUE, 
           color.blocks = c('darkorchid', 'brown1', 'lightgreen'),
           color.cor = c("chocolate3","grey20"), 
           size.labels = 1.2, size.variables = 0.5, size.legend = 1)

# Interpretation:
# - Each arc represents one omics block with selected variables
# - Lines connecting variables show strong correlations (|r| > 0.9)
# - Clusters of connected variables represent coordinated multi-omics modules
# - These modules may represent co-regulated biological pathways
```

## Save 
```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=10}
# Export DIABLO network for visualization in Cytoscape
# Cytoscape provides advanced network layout and styling options
# Reference: http://mixomics.org/graphics/variable-plots/network/

# Create network object from DIABLO model
# network() extracts correlation network between selected variables
# blocks = c(1,2,3): include all three omics blocks (Transcript, Protein, Metabolite_GC)
# cutoff = 0.9: only include edges (correlations) with |r| > 0.9
myNetwork <- network(final.diablo.model, blocks = c(1,2,3), cutoff = 0.9) 

# Export network to GML format (Graph Modeling Language)
# GML files can be imported into Cytoscape for interactive visualization
# The network includes:
# - Nodes: selected variables from each omics block
# - Edges: strong correlations (|r| > 0.9) between variables
# - Node attributes: omics type, variable name, contribution values
# - Edge attributes: correlation coefficients
write_graph(myNetwork$gR, 
            file = "/Users/wmujchariyak/Desktop/myNetwork_conserved_Strep.gml", 
            format = "gml")

# Next step: Import this GML file into Cytoscape (see 3_Cytoscape_Strep_081025.R)
# for advanced network visualization, clustering, and annotation
```
